lessons.sourceTeacherGoal: Determine whether statements about data are true or false. Write statements about data from a visual representation.
lessons.sourceStudentTask: Evaluate true/false statements about an illustrated pet-survey tally chart; write three separate observations, then choose a centre.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Worked model — lesson skill
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: Our sample pet chart shows 6 cats, 4 dogs and 2 fish. Is 'More chose cats than dogs' true?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Yes. Six is greater than four. Twelve children are represented in this fictional chart.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Try one more — a different lesson-skill problem
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: Write two true observations and correct one false observation about the pet chart.
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Six children chose cats. Two children chose fish. 'Four chose cats' is false: four chose dogs.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Check with another representation
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How could you show the same answer using counters or a written calculation?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Use these labeled groups: Cats — 6; Dogs — 4; Fish — 2. Count six cat marks and four dog marks; the difference is two. 6+4+2=12.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Explain the diagram to a partner
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How can the diagram help you explain this lesson's worked model?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Name which group represents each number and explain the comparison or change. Count six cat marks and four dog marks; the difference is two. 6+4+2=12.

lessons.sourceTeacherGoal: Answer “how many in each category” and “how many in all” questions about data represented in different ways.
lessons.sourceStudentTask: Read tally-mark and numeric category tables, count categories individually, combine two groups, and find the survey total.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Worked model — lesson skill
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: Seven apples and three bananas were counted. How many fruits are in all?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: 10 fruits.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Try one more — a different lesson-skill problem
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: The tally chart has seven apples and three bananas. How many more apples than bananas?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: 4 more apples.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Check with another representation
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How could you show the same answer using counters or a written calculation?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Use these labeled groups: Apples: first five; Apples: two more; Bananas: three. Seven equals a group of five plus two; 7+3=10.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Explain the diagram to a partner
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How can the diagram help you explain this lesson's worked model?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Name which group represents each number and explain the comparison or change. Seven equals a group of five plus two; 7+3=10.

lessons.sourceTeacherGoal: Build toward fluency by adding and subtracting within 10 in a way that makes sense to them. Sort objects into categories and represent the sort.
lessons.sourceStudentTask: Practise counting plus/minus two and select an arithmetic/sort-display centre.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Worked model — lesson skill
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: Sort 12 classroom objects: 5 counters, 4 tiles and 3 blocks. How many objects are displayed?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: 12 objects.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Try one more — a different lesson-skill problem
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: In the example sort of five counters, four tiles and three blocks, which category has two more items than blocks?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Counters. Five counters is two more than three blocks.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Check with another representation
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How could you show the same answer using counters or a written calculation?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Use these labeled groups: Counters — 5; Tiles — 4; Blocks — 3. 5+4+3=12. Every one of the twelve objects belongs to one labeled row.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Explain the diagram to a partner

lessons.sourceTeacherGoal: Collect, organize, and represent data from survey questions. Create questions related to survey data. Interpret data to answer questions.
lessons.sourceStudentTask: Choose a survey question, collect ten participant responses, author questions about the collected data, and create a poster.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Worked model — lesson skill
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: A practice survey records 4 votes for monkeys, 3 for lions and 2 for parrots. How many choices are recorded?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: 9 choices.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Try one more — a different lesson-skill problem
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: Write a survey question with the three animal choices. How would you collect actual replies?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Which jungle animal would you most like to see: monkey, lion or parrot? Ask each person once and tally their one choice.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Check with another representation
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How could you show the same answer using counters or a written calculation?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Use these labeled groups: Monkey — 4; Lion — 3; Parrot — 2. 4+3+2=9; one mark means one response. This does not claim nine real classmates were asked.

candidateWorkedExamples.Title: Explain the diagram to a partner
candidateWorkedExamples.Question: How can the diagram help you explain this lesson's worked model?
candidateWorkedExamples.Answer: Name which group represents each number and explain the comparison or change. 4+3+2=9; one mark means one response. This does not claim nine real classmates were asked.
